title: Passed Over at the Bank, Folorunsho Alakija Went to Study Fashion
dek: A Lagos bank secretary who had risen to head corporate affairs saw graduates promoted past her, resigned, and launched a fashion label that won a national award within weeks.

story.company: Supreme Stitches (later Rose of Sharon House of Fashion)
story.event: Leaving a twelve-year banking career after being passed over for graduates, studying fashion abroad and launching Supreme Stitches
story.summary: Folorunsho Alakija joined First National Bank of Chicago (later International Merchant Bank of Nigeria) in Lagos as a secretary in the 1970s and rose to head corporate affairs and work in treasury. After about twelve years, seeing graduates ranked and promoted above her, she resigned, studied fashion design in London with her two youngest children in tow, and launched Supreme Stitches; three weeks later she was named Fashion Designer of the Year 1986. The label became the Rose of Sharon House of Fashion in 1996.
paragraphs: In the treasury department of the International Merchant Bank of Nigeria in Lagos, Folorunsho Alakija once asked herself a plain question: how long would it take to go from treasury officer to general manager? She had joined the bank, then First National Bank of Chicago, as a secretary in the 1970s, become executive secretary to the managing director and later headed corporate affairs. On the bank's in-house banking course she had been the only person without a university degree. "My result came out well and I was very proud," she recalled.

The answer was discouraging. The bank, she said later, began "putting extra cogs between the wheels", and she watched new intakes being ranked and promoted above her. She did not feel inferior, she told Vanguard in 2012, but she was frustrated, because she believed she would prove herself if given the chance. She did not blame the bank, which she said was "capitalising on degrees." After about twelve years there, by her own estimate, she resigned.

What she chose was fashion, a trade she had known since childhood, when she and her siblings helped in her mother's textile store. She went abroad to study design, at the American College in London and the Central School of Fashion, where she earned a distinction. Her husband, Modupe, a lawyer, agreed on one condition: that she take the youngest two of their four children with her. The youngest, a son, was two years old.

Back in Nigeria she launched her own label. "Precisely three weeks after I formally launched my label, Supreme Stitches," she said, "I won a national award as the Fashion Designer of the Year 1986." Her clients came to include the former first lady Maryam Babangida. In 1996 the label was renamed the Rose of Sharon House of Fashion. By then she had also, in May 1993, applied for an oil prospecting licence, the beginning of the business that later made her, on Forbes's 2015 ranking, the richest woman in Nigeria.

quote.text: He is like a ship in a river; he runs against obstructions on every side but one, on that side all obstruction is taken away and he sweeps serenely over a deepening channel into an infinite sea.
quote.source_title: Essays — First Series, Project Gutenberg eBook #2944
quote.connection: Emerson pictures a vocation as the one side of the river where obstruction falls away. Looking back, Alakija's turn to fashion fits the image. At the moment she resigned, though, she could see the obstruction clearly and the open channel not at all.

reflection: Alakija did not leave because she disliked banking; she had done well there. She left after an honest sum about a ladder whose rungs had been moved, and she did not need the bank to be a villain to justify going.

Emerson makes it sound as if the open channel announces itself. It rarely does at the moment of choosing. What Alakija had was a skill learned in her mother's shop, a condition to meet at home and two small children on the journey. If you are weighing a sum of your own about where your present path leads, it is worth doing on paper, on a calm morning, rather than at the end of a frustrating day.
invitation: Write down one honest estimate: how long, on your present path, until you reach the thing you are working towards. Then ask one person who knows that path whether your number looks right.

cross_checks.claim: Alakija spent about twelve years at the bank, rising from secretary to head of corporate affairs and work in treasury.
She left because promotion was being blocked or given to graduates ahead of her.
She studied fashion design at the American College in London and the Central School of Fashion.
Supreme Stitches was her first label, and she won a national design award soon after launching it.
The label was renamed the Rose of Sharon House of Fashion in 1996.

research_notes: Dates do not fit neatly. Vanguard (2011) has her hired in mid-1974 by First National Bank of Chicago; ThisDay, BusinessDay and Forbes Africa (via CNBC Africa) say she first spent time at Sijuade Enterprises from 1974, Forbes Africa saying about a year and a half. She puts her bank years at 'about 12', which from the mid-1970s would run to about 1986-87, yet she says she won Fashion Designer of the Year 1986 three weeks after launching Supreme Stitches, after studying abroad. The story therefore gives no year for her resignation, says 'about twelve years ... by her own estimate', and uses 1986 only for the award; approx_date is 1986 rather than the slate's 1985. Bank name: the bank she joined was First National Bank of Chicago, which sources describe as becoming the International Merchant Bank of Nigeria (later FinBank); Forbes Africa calls it IMB throughout; the story names both. Where she studied: the 2012 Vanguard interview says only 'abroad'; the 2011 interview says England; Forbes Africa, ThisDay and BusinessDay name the American College in London and the Central School of Fashion. ThisDay calls the 1986 honour a contest she won; she calls it a national award; the story uses her words. Funding: no source says how Supreme Stitches was financed (the 2011 interview says she had invested her salary in shares and property, but does not link this to the label), so funding is 'unknown', not the slate's 'bootstrapped'. Her remark that she 'didn't feel inferior' ends with an exclamation mark in the source, so it is paraphrased rather than quoted. The Punch interview (2021), The Guardian (Nigeria) and BlackPast could not be read or returned 403 and are not cited.
